Mitigation Proposal:

Mechanism: Closed-loop, feedforward correction of die pressure oscillations via dynamic speed modulation. The core insight is that film gauge is inversely proportional to extrusion rate (mass flow) and directly proportional to the die pressure gradient; oscillating die pressure causes periodic gauge variation. Since the line-speed encoder provides real-time velocity data and the melt pressure transducer provides the driving pressure, we can use the existing sensors to compute a real-time, high-bandwidth estimate of the melt flow rate (approximated by pressure divided by a calibrated impedance coefficient, or by integrating pressure over time to estimate volume flow). By dynamically adjusting the line speed (traction speed) in anti-phase to the detected pressure oscillation, we maintain a constant mass flow rate through the die, thereby stabilizing the exit velocity and gauge profile. This decouples the gauge from the pressure instability by actively compensating for it through speed control, which is a standard technique for handling upstream disturbances in extrusion when only limited sensors are available.

DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: The driving variable is the oscillating die pressure signal (P_osc). An increase in die pressure causes an increase in melt volumetric flow rate through the die, which, if uncorrected, results in a decrease in film gauge (thinning) at the take-off. The control action applies a positive correction to the line-speed command (ΔV) that is in-phase with the pressure increase. This increases the traction speed, pulling more material through the die, which counteracts the thinning tendency and stabilizes the gauge at the target thickness. Conversely, a decrease in die pressure triggers a negative correction to line speed, preventing over-thickening. The net effect is that the gauge variation (output) is driven toward the setpoint by modulating the line speed (input) in response to die pressure (disturbance/measurement).

Implementation:
1.  Signal Conditioning & Filtering: Take the raw signal from the melt pressure transducer (P_melt). Apply a band-pass filter (e.g., 1–10 Hz) to isolate the oscillatory component responsible for the gauge variation, rejecting low-frequency drift and high-frequency noise. Simultaneously, take the raw signal from the line-speed encoder (V_actual) and use it directly as the reference/feedback signal for the speed loop. The melt temperature transducer signal (T_melt) is low-pass filtered to capture slow viscosity drifts.
2.  Controller Design: Implement a Proportional-Integral (PI) control loop. The input to this controller is the filtered, high-frequency component of the melt pressure oscillation (P_filt). The output of this controller is a correction signal (ΔV) added to the base line-speed setpoint. The gain of this controller is tuned so that when die pressure increases, the controller increases the line speed command. The temperature signal (T_melt) is used to adaptively scale the gain (gain-scheduling) to account for viscosity changes, ensuring the pressure-to-flow relationship remains constant.
3.  Execution: The computed total speed command (V_setpoint = V_base + ΔV) is sent to the existing line-speed drive inverter. The drive adjusts the traction roller speed to match this new command in real-time. The existing sensors (pressure, temperature, speed encoder) provide the necessary feedback for this closed loop; no new sensors are installed.

Measures Relied Upon (Source & Derivation):
*   Melt Pressure Transducer: Provides P_melt directly. Derived signal P_filt = BandPass(P_melt, 1-10Hz) is used as the controller error signal.
*   Line-Speed Encoder: Provides V_actual directly. Used as the feedback for the outer speed loop and to verify the drive is tracking the command.
*   Melt Temperature Transducers: Provides T_melt directly. Derived signal T_avg = Average(T_melt_transducers) is used to determine the viscosity correction factor for gain scaling.
*   Existing Line-Speed Drive: Actuator. Input is the command V_setpoint.
